summary:
Mars Walker is a full-stack, terrain-aware route planning and 3D traverse simulation platform for Jezero Crater on Mars. We turned raw USGS CTX elevation data and NASA HiRISE imagery into a living routing system, from data pipeline to interactive 3D.

What we built:

A resumable geospatial pipeline. Pinned, SHA-256-verified source rasters are processed in bounded chunks into a 100 m routing graph in PostgreSQL, PostGIS, and pgRouting. Interrupted builds pick up exactly where they stopped.
Profile-based routing. Each cell is scored by slope, traversability, and hazard clearance. The rover and the suited astronaut (30° slopes, 30 m hazard buffer) get their own cost models, and routes are cached for instant replay.
Side-by-side comparison. Both walkers are computed in parallel and compared by distance, slope, hazards, and estimated mission time.
A realistic mission simulation. Walker-specific speed models, work cycles, Martian solar time, and a sun that follows the mission clock.
A 3D Explorer. Built with React, MapLibre, and three.js, it puts you on the ground with four nested terrain levels, native 1 m HiRISE terrain, NASA’s official Perseverance model with spinning wheels, procedural rocks, and real Perseverance raw images.
details:
Mars Walker is like Google Maps for Mars. You choose a traveler (the Perseverance rover or a suited astronaut), click a start and a destination in Jezero Crater, and get a terrain-aware route.

Mars has no roads, so we built the map from the terrain itself. A resumable pipeline downloads checksum-verified USGS CTX elevation data and processes it in bounded chunks into a 100 m routing graph in PostgreSQL, PostGIS, and pgRouting. Each cell is scored by slope, traversability, and hazard clearance, and each walker has its own cost profile. The astronaut handles slopes up to 30° and keeps 30 m from hazards, while the rover slows by up to 65% on steep ground.

A Compare mode computes both routes in parallel and shows distance, slope, hazards, and estimated mission time side by side. Start runs a mission simulation using walker-specific speeds, work cycles, and Martian Local Mean Solar Time. The 3D Explorer then puts you on the ground, on native 1 m HiRISE terrain, with NASA's official Perseverance model.

What benefits does it have?

Anyone can understand and explore a traverse without GIS expertise.

Computed routes are cached, so saved routes open instantly.

The whole system starts with one command, make start.

Rover and astronaut routes can be compared on the same terrain.

What is the intended impact?

To make planetary exploration easier to understand and teach. It can serve as an educational and outreach tool, and as a foundation for exploring how different explorers would cross the same terrain. It is a demonstration only and is not certified for mission or human safety.

Tools and technologies

Data: USGS CTX, NASA/USGS HiRISE, the USGS geologic map, and Perseverance raw images from NASA's public API.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, PostGIS, pgRouting, and TiTiler for raster tiles.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, MapLibre, and three.js (react-three-fiber).

Infrastructure: Docker Compose, Make, and Dev Containers.

Hardware: no special hardware, just a regular machine with about 12 GB of free disk space.

How is it creative?

It applies the familiar "navigation app" idea to another planet, with travelers that have physically different limits.

The 3D Explorer uses four nested terrain levels with no seams, a Perseverance model whose wheels spin independently, rocks placed from the orthoimage's roughness, and a sky that follows the Martian time of day.

Simulation time can be warped up to 100,000×, so a traverse takes minutes to watch instead of hours.

What factors did our team consider?

Reliability: pinned downloads with SHA-256 checks, plus graph builds that resume from the last committed chunk after interruptions.

Scalability: memory stays bounded, since it grows with the chunk size and not with the full graph.

Reproducibility: graphs are tied to a dataset version, so only outdated profiles are rebuilt.

Graceful degradation: if the HiRISE data or rover model is missing, the app falls back to CTX terrain and a procedural rover.

Honesty about limits: on the 100 m grid the two walkers often share a path, so the difference is mostly mission time. We clearly label the project as a demonstration.

Safety and realism: hazard buffers, slope limits, and work-hour constraints per walker.
